title: This Space Peanut Wobbles Like a Top!
summary: Imagine a space rock shaped like a peanut, tumbling through the asteroid belt. That's what NASA's Lucy spacecraft found when it zoomed past an asteroid called Donaldjohanson last year! Instead of spinning neatly like a top, this asteroid wobbles — it flips end-over-end once every 10.5 days and sways back and forth every 26.5 days. Scientists say it's like a wobbly toy top that just won't stay still. The asteroid is about the size of a small town, and its peanut shape comes from two chunks that gently stuck together after a big crash 155 million years ago. That's young for an asteroid — many are billions of years old! Lucy's cameras also spotted ridges and craters, and even signs that water once flowed there, but only for a short time. The Sun's heat is slowly changing how the asteroid spins, a weird effect that can speed up or slow down space rocks. This flyby was just a practice run for Lucy's main mission: visiting Jupiter's Trojan asteroids in 2027. Those ancient rocks could tell us how the planets formed. For now, Donaldjohanson is giving scientists a rare peek at a young, wobbly world.
why_it_matters: Learning about asteroids helps us understand where Earth came from — and one day, knowing how they move could help protect our planet from a dangerous crash.

background_read: NASA (the U.S. space agency) built the Lucy spacecraft to explore asteroids, which are rocky leftovers from when the planets formed billions of years ago.
The asteroid belt sits between Mars and Jupiter — it's like a giant ring of millions of space rocks, some tiny and some as big as small towns.
Donaldjohanson is named after a scientist who studied ancient human bones; Trojan asteroids (space rocks trapped near Jupiter's orbit) might hold clues about Earth's own beginnings.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA's Lucy spacecraft and scientists studying space rocks
WHAT: Found that asteroid Donaldjohanson wobbles, has ridges and craters, and once had water flowing on it
WHERE: In the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, on the way to Jupiter's Trojan asteroids
WHY: The flyby was practice for a bigger 2027 mission to study ancient Trojan asteroids and learn how the planets formed

perspectives.description: Scientists are thrilled because Donaldjohanson is a rare young asteroid — only 155 million years old — so it's like getting a baby photo of a space rock. Every wobble and crater teaches them something new.
A wobbly, tumbling asteroid is much harder to map and predict than a steady one. Researchers have to work extra hard to understand what Lucy's pictures really show.
This flyby wasn't even the main event — it was a warm-up. The team wanted to test Lucy's cameras and systems before the bigger mission in 2027, making sure everything works far from Earth.
